notes.4: Parses the request URL so query parameters can be read.
notes.5: Reads the `expr` query parameter — fully attacker-controlled.
notes.8: Sends the computed result back to the client.
notes.11: Starts the HTTP server on port 3000.

options.label: `eval` is slow, so many requests degrade performance
options.whyWrong: Performance is irrelevant; the problem is that the input is executed as code.

options.label: `expr` is passed to `eval`, so any JavaScript in it runs with the server's privileges
`String(result)` can throw when the result is an object
options.whyWrong: A formatting error is trivial next to arbitrary code execution.

options.label: Run eval inside a try/catch so errors don't crash the server
options.whyWrong: Catching errors does nothing to stop the attacker's code from executing first.

options.label: Parse the expression with a dedicated math parser instead of eval
options.diff:
-  const result = eval(expr);
+  const result = evaluateArithmetic(expr); // a real parser, no code execution

options.label: Cast expr to a number before evaluating
options.diff:
-  const result = eval(expr);
+  const result = eval(Number(expr));
options.whyWrong: `Number(expr)` of a non-numeric string is NaN, and this still calls eval — the pattern is unchanged.

options.label: Set the response content type to text/plain
options.whyWrong: Response headers have nothing to do with executing the input.

training.exploit: Request `?expr=process.mainModule.require('child_process').execSync('id').toString()`. `eval` runs it, so the server executes `id` (or any command) and returns the output — full remote code execution.

hints.line: Find where user input is executed rather than just used.
hints.fix: Never eval user input — parse it instead.

writeup.summary: `eval(expr)` executes the query parameter as JavaScript in the server process. Anything the Node runtime can do — read files, spawn processes, open sockets — an attacker can do by sending it as `expr`. The fix is to never pass untrusted input to `eval`; evaluate arithmetic with a dedicated parser that treats the input purely as data.
